html:
The Slavery Abolition Act, passed by the British Parliament in 1833 and in force from 1 August 1834, ended slavery in most of the British Empire. It freed about 800,000 enslaved people, most of them in Caribbean colonies such as Jamaica, plus the Cape Colony and Mauritius.

It capped a campaign of half a century. Activists such as William Wilberforce and Thomas Clarkson first won the ban on the slave trade in 1807, ending Britain's part in the Atlantic slave trade. Revolts by the enslaved pushed things on, above all the great Jamaican rising of 1831 to 1832 known as the Baptist War.

Freedom came with strings. Former slaves over six had to work as unpaid "apprentices" until 1838. The owners, not the enslaved, were paid compensation of 20 million pounds, about 40 percent of the government's yearly spending. Lands of the East India Company were left out at first. Planters soon turned to indentured workers from India to replace the lost labour.
